Key hazards
  • Rainfall: Tropical Depression Nine is expected to produce rainfall amounts of 2 to 4 inches through Thursday across coastal portions of the Bay of Campeche with isolated higher amounts possible in the states of Campeche and western Yucatan. From Friday through the weekend, the system is expected to produce rainfall amounts of 3 to 6 inches, with localized totals up to 10 inches, across the central U.S. Gulf Coast extending from southeastern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle. Flash and urban flooding, along with isolated river flooding, will be possible. For a complete depiction of forecast rainfall associated with Tropical Depression Nine, please see the National Weather Service Storm Total Rainfall Graphic available at hurricanes.gov/graphics_at4.shtml?rainqpf and the Flash Flood Risk graphic at hurricanes.gov/graphics_at4.shtml?ero.
  • Wind: Gusty winds are possible in portions of the Yucatan Peninsula on Thursday.
  • Surf: Swells generated by the depression are expected to affect the western and northern portions of the Yucatan Peninsula beginning on Thursday. These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions. Please consult products from your local weather office. A depiction of rip current risk for the United States can be found at: hurricanes.gov/graphics_at4.shtml?ripCurrents

Sources & how this was made

Why this page exists

It is Jim's personal hurricane check for home in Clearwater, FL (Pinellas County). It puts the threat first: is anything likely to affect land within 72 hours, and how close is it to Clearwater / Tampa Bay — then the rest of the Atlantic, Pacific and West Pacific for context.

How it is built

  1. Every 3 hours a scheduled job runs refresh_storm_dash.sh on a private workstation.
  2. Python scripts download the official products listed below straight from NOAA's National Hurricane Center (NHC/CPHC), the National Weather Service (NWS) and the Joint Typhoon Warning Center (JTWC) — text advisories, outlooks and the NHC GIS shapefiles (cone, track, forecast points, past track, outlook areas, watch/warning lines).
  3. The scripts rank systems by threat to the US / Florida, draw the static maps, and build this page. The interactive map's shapes are embedded in the page at build time (no live data calls), so it is a snapshot as of the pulled time shown.
  4. The page is published to GitHub Pages (a static web host) and checked live after each refresh.

Official vs. calculated

  • Official (copied from NHC/NWS/JTWC): storm positions, winds, pressure, movement, forecast points and times, cones, outlook areas and formation odds, watches/warnings, wind-speed probabilities, NWS alerts and discussion text.
  • Calculated by this dashboard (not official): distances and bearings from Clearwater/Tampa, the distance line, "closest forecast point", plain-language positions ("about 400 mi W of…"), estimated coast-crossing times interpolated between NHC forecast points, threat ranking and the CLEAR / MONITOR / WATCH / WARNING status labels (those labels follow NWS watches/warnings when any exist).
  • Duplicate check: when an outlook invest (e.g. Invest AL92) becomes an advisory storm (e.g. TD Nine, AL09), the old invest entry is dropped automatically. Nothing needed dropping this run.
  • Fetch problems this run: none — every source above downloaded and parsed.

Limitations

  • This is not an official warning source. It can be up to 3 hours old, a download can fail, and parsing can be wrong. Always follow the National Hurricane Center (nhc.noaa.gov), NWS Tampa Bay (weather.gov/tbw) and Pinellas County Emergency Management (evacuation zones, shelters: Pinellas Hurricane Guide).
  • The cone shows where the storm's center will probably go — not how big the storm is. Surge, wind and rain often reach far outside it.
  • Formation odds are chances a depression or storm forms, not landfall odds. Disturbances have no official track until NHC starts advisories.
  • Times are converted to Eastern Time. GTWO outlook GIS stamp: Tue Oct 6, 7:29 PM ET.
